after.title: Preprint: Defining Constructs of Hand Function Quality at Home After Cervical Spinal Cord Injury Through Egocentric Videos: A Qualitative Inquiry
after.authors: Naoreen, A.; Bajwa, T.; Unger, J.; Zariffa, J.
after.abstract: Introduction: Loss of hand function is an impactful consequence of cervical spinal cord injury (cSCI), affecting activities of daily living (ADLs). Hand function assessments play an important role in developing interventions that mitigate these impacts. However, assessment can be complicated by factors including the diversity of grasps and use of assistive devices. Consequently, standardized assessments in clinical environments do not fully reflect function in real-world settings. This gap has resulted in increasing interest in assessing hand function at home through wearable cameras (egocentric video) to provide information about real-world hand use. Despite advancements, a framework is required to describe the quality of hand use when observing unconstrained tasks through egocentric video. This study aimed to define constructs that describe hand function quality in unconstrained, in-home activities after cSCI, captured through egocentric videos. Methods: A qualitative study was conducted using focus groups (N=17) to generate a list of constructs defining good quality hand use in unconstrained environments after cSCI through egocentric videos. Individuals with cSCI, physicians, therapists, and researchers participated. Content analysis was used to identify patterns, codes and categories. Results: Fourteen categories and thirty-three constructs were identified. While several constructs were common across groups, distinct perspectives also emerged highlighting the multidimensional nature of hand function. Discussion: Perceptions of meaningful hand function encompass a broad range of constructs, emphasizing the importance of both functional performance and motor control aspects. The identified constructs provide a basis for the development of novel metrics of hand function in the context of real-world ADLs.

after.title: Preprint: Effects of an exercise prescription system (ACTIVE) on physical function in community-dwelling older adults: protocol for a single-centre, assessor-blinded, parallel-group randomised controlled trial
after.authors: Pan, Y.; Liu, H.; Li, Y.; Hao, Y.; Qing, M.; Wang, Z.; Miao, X.; Xu, Y.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Sports Medicine, Beijing Key Laboratory of Sports Injuries,  Peking University Third Hospital
after.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction China is experiencing rapid population ageing and has the largest elderly population in the world. Physical exercise is one of the core strategies for promoting healthy ageing, and digital, intelligent exercise interventions hold promise as important tools for healthy ageing; however, clinical evidence remains limited. Methods and analysis This study is a single centre, assessor blinded, parallel group randomised controlled trial (RCT) designed to evaluate the effects of a knowledge rule based artificial intelligence exercise decision making programme (ACTIVE) on improving physical function in older adults, compared with a standardised, nonpersonalised exercise programme. A total of 142 older adults will be recruited in Beijing and randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to either the ACTIVE group (n=71) or the standardised, non-personalised exercise training group (n=71) for an 8-week intervention. The primary outcome is the composite physical function Z score at week 8 (derived from the unweighted average of standardised scores for 4 metre gait speed, 5 times chair stand time, 6 minute walk distance, and single leg stance time); secondary outcomes include the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), EQ5D5L, PHQ-9 depression score, objective physical activity (accelerometry), and muscle strength, among others. Ethics and dissemination This study has been approved by the Medical Science Research Ethics Committee of Peking University Third Hospital (2025) Medical Ethics Review No. (991 01). Study results will be disseminated through peer reviewed journal publications and academic conferences. Trial registration ChiCTR2600117481 Strengths and limitations of this study 1.This study develops and evaluates a knowledge rule based artificial intelligence exercise decision making programme (ACTIVE), forming a closed loop intervention cycle of "assessment decision execution feedback", which represents a degree of methodological innovation. 2.The intervention is delivered via a WeChat mini programme combined with centralised randomisation and a home based training setting, demonstrating good real world feasibility and potential for scalability. 3.This study adopts a composite physical function Z-score comprising 4 metre gait speed, 5 times chair stand time, 6 minute walk distance, and single leg stance time as the primary outcome, which more comprehensively reflects overall physical function changes in relatively healthy older adults and reduces the ceiling effect associated with single item measures. 4.As this study involves a behavioural exercise intervention, blinding of participants and intervention providers is not possible, which may introduce performance bias and expectation bias. 5.The intervention period is 8 weeks, primarily intended to assess the preliminary effects of the ACTIVE programme; the long term maintenance of these effects cannot be determined from this study alone.

after.title: Preprint: A report-supervised EEG-language foundation model enables broad, interactive clinical interpretation
after.authors: Kranz, D. D.; Terziev, R.; Lukomksi, M.; Krumm, L. M.; Meisel, C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Section on Computational Neurology, Berlin Institute of Health and Department of Neurology, Charite - Universitatsmedizin Berlin
after.abstract: Medical AI for complex signals such as electroencephalography (EEG) relies on costly expert annotations and predefined diagnostic labels that fail to capture the richness and nuance of clinical interpretation. Whether models trained on routine clinical reports can overcome these limitations while matching expert-supervised performance remains unclear. We introduce EEG Copilot, a biosignal-language foundation model trained on routine EEG-report pairs without dedicated task-specific expert annotations. Across two external datasets (6,078 EEGs), EEG Copilot performed on par with a state-of-the-art expert-supervised model across 11 shared findings (mean AUROC 0.80-0.81), corroborated by direct neurologist review of 200 EEGs. Beyond predefined diagnostic categories in conventional EEG AI, EEG Copilot assessed 23 clinical characteristics through natural-language questions in English and German across 9,689 EEGs from four hospitals (mean AUROC 0.80-0.82), demonstrating that automated EEG assessment need no longer be confined to fixed diagnostic outputs. Crucially, EEG Copilot generated integrated clinical impressions directly from EEG rather than isolated predictions with shuffled-report controls supporting recording-specific content and neurologist review of 800 impressions showing that most were accurate or clinically usable with minor errors. These findings chart a path beyond label-bound medical AI, transforming routine clinical reports into scalable supervision for flexible, language-driven assessment and integrated interpretation of complex physiological signals.

after.title: Preprint: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis progression is tracked in plasma by systemic proteins independent of motor neurons
after.authors: Finney, C.; Shvetcov, A.
after.abstract: Blood biomarkers that change as patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) decline would allow progression to be monitored more objectively. Plasma proteomic studies have identified proteins that differ between patients and controls, but which plasma proteins change as patients decline, and whether they come from motor neurons, is unknown. Here, we leveraged the Answer ALS cohort, with serial SomaScan plasma proteomics, repeated ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised assessments, and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons (iMNs) from the same patients. At baseline, 77 plasma proteins differed between 245 patients and 76 controls. These were dominated by muscle proteins, including PDLIM3, ACTN2, and MYOM2, and reflected disease severity. Using a two-stage longitudinal design, we identified 72 progression markers whose within-patient change tracked the rate of functional decline, led by CLEC3B, ANTXR2, and ART3. These were largely distinct from the most elevated muscle proteins and were secreted or shed proteins spread across many tissues. Both sets replicated in the independent Target ALS cohort. A motor neuron expression map built from the iMNs showed that motor neuron proteins were underrepresented in both sets and that expression in iMNs did not predict tracking of decline. Baseline serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) predicted how quickly patients declined but its change did not track decline, whereas change in the progression markers did so within every stratum of baseline NfL. Neither tracked decline in the fastest progressing patients. This positions baseline NfL for prognosis and stratification and systemic plasma proteins for monitoring.

after.title: Preprint: Exploring the genetic determinants of ALS in a North Indian cohort using a genomic screening approach
after.authors: Roychowdhury, S.; Joshi, D.; Kumar, A.; Das, P.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Centre for Genetic Disorders, Institute of Science, Banaras Hindu University
after.abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a clinically and genetically heterogenous neurodegenerative disorder in which both monogenic and complex genetic mechanism contribute to disease susceptibility. Increasing evidence also indicates that non motor manifestations, including sleep disturbances, significantly influence disease burden. This study aimed to characterize the genetic spectrum of ALS in a predominantly North Indian cohort while evaluating the prevalence of sleep related abnormalities. Methods: Seventy-three clinically diagnosed ALS patients were recruited from a tertiary care centre in North India. Disease severity was assessed using the ALSFRS-R. Sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, and REM sleep behaviour disorder symptoms were evaluated using the PSQI, ESS and RBDQ questionnaires, respectively. Genetic analysis included targeted sequencing of SOD1, TARDBP, and ANG, followed by repeat expansion analysis of C9orf72, ATXN1, ATXN2, ATXN3, and ATXN7. Whole exome sequencing was performed in selected cases to further investigate the genetic basis of ALS. Results: The cohort demonstrated a male predominance and an earlier age of onset compared to many Western populations. Poor sleep quality and excessive daytime sleepiness were frequently observed although no significant association was found between sleep parameters and disease severity. Genetic screening identified a pathogenic/likely pathogenic TARDBP variant classified by ClinVar while no known or novel pathogenic variants were detected in SOD1 or ANG. Repeat expansion studies revealed one patient harbouring pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansions. For the ATXN1, one patient harboured pathogenic repeat expansions and two patients carried intermediate length repeats. Additionally, one patient harboured intermediate repeat expansions in ATXN2. Whole exome sequencing revealed novel and rare variants in ALS associated genes including ANXA11, SIGMAR1, SETX, ERBB4 and NEK1, highlighting substantial genetic heterogeneity. Conclusions: Our findings highlight the complex genetic heterogeneity of ALS, with pathogenic repeat expansions and rare variants identified across multiple disease associated genes. These results demonstrate the importance of comprehensive genetic testing to improve the detection of clinically relevant variants in ALS. In addition, the high prevalence of sleep related disturbances observed in the cohort emphasizes the need to incorporate non motor assessment into routine clinical evaluation of patients with ALS.

after.authors: Kabanga, R. L.; Watts, G. L.; Chambo, V. J.; Benela, Z.; Maembe, L.; Haidar, T.
after.abstract: Background: Caesarean delivery can be lifesaving when clinically indicated, but high facility rates require regular audit to distinguish appropriate emergency obstetric care from potentially avoidable operative delivery. This study described caesarean delivery patterns and selected maternal-neonatal outcomes among women delivering at Mwananyamala Regional Referral Hospital in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Methods: A retrospective record review was conducted using complete delivery records from January 2025 to June 2025. The analytic dataset included 302 eligible records abstracted from delivery registers, admission records, and neonatal logs. The primary outcome was caesarean delivery. Associations were assessed using logistic regression restricted to variables available before or at the time of delivery decision. Post-delivery variables were not treated as predictors of caesarean delivery. Gestational-age values below 28 weeks or missing values were treated as invalid/missing and excluded from the study.  Results: Mean maternal age was 28.09 {+/-} 6.68 years; 9.93% were <20 years, 68.87% were 20-34 years and 21.19% were [≥]35 years. Most women were multiparous (53.3%) and 43.71% delivered by caesarean section. In multivariable analysis, caesarean delivery was associated with employment (AOR=3.54; P<0.001), primigravity (AOR=2.65; P=0.009), prior uterine scar (AOR=1.89; P=0.002), and high-risk pregnancies (AOR=2.68; P=0.003). Maternal complications were infrequent, but postpartum hemorrhage was more common among older mothers. Neonatal outcomes were largely favorable, with 92.4% live births and 15.2% low birth weight.  Conclusion: Caesarean delivery was common among complete records at this urban referral hospital, but maternal age was not an independent predictor. The results support routine caesarean-delivery audit, improved delivery-register documentation, and future Robson-classification analysis once the necessary variables are captured reliably.

after.abstract: Background: An increasing number of women in the UK enter into pregnancy with high BMI (BMI [≥]30kg/m2). On a population level, higher BMI is associated with an increased risk of pregnancy complications. However, many women experience communication from healthcare professionals about BMI-related risk as unsatisfactory. We aimed to explore how these dicussions could be made more acceptable by understanding how pregnant women with high BMI perceive, experience, and receive communication about their health and risk mitigation. Methods: We recruited women with a booking BMI [≥]30kg/m2 from an antenatal ward at a tertiary maternity unit in the UK. Individual interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed. Data was analysed according to practical thematic analysis using qualitative analysis software. Results: Our analysis (n=15 participants) revealed that BMI-related risk discourse resulted in a range of negative emotions, which aligned to four major themes: (i) BMI is unhelpful as a metric of health, (ii) 'healthy pregnancy' is not determined by BMI, (iii) BMI-related risk is emotionally burdensome, and (iv) desire to personalise BMI-related risk. Pregnant women with high BMI did not perceive themselves or their pregnancies as unhealthy and did not necessarily desire additional support or investigations in pregnancy. Women reported that maternity staff emphasised BMI-related risk but gave little information on (i) what risk means for the individual, (ii) how to reduce BMI-related risk, and (iii) why interventions are offered, and (iv) how they can be declined. Conclusion: Risk mitigation and health communication may be more acceptable to pregnant women with high BMI when it acknowledges the uncertainties and limitations of BMI, prioritises outcomes and gives information that matters to women with high BMI, and avoids weight-related stigma.

after.title: Preprint: The Impact of Hurricane Helene on the Incidence of Acute Gastrointestinal Illness in North Carolina, US: A Controlled Interrupted Time Series Analysis
after.authors: Liddie, J. M.; O'Brien, K. R.; Pasha, A.; Iseson, A.; Apanasovich, T. V.; Bagchi, P.; Pastwa, A.; Hu, X. C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The George Washington Milken Institute School of Public Health
after.abstract: In September 2024, Hurricane Helene caused significant flooding in western North Carolina (NC), leading to concerns surrounding water quality, including the risk of acute gastrointestinal illness (AGI). The potential for flooding-related drinking water contamination is exacerbated for private well users, who comprised a large proportion of the population most affected by the hurricane. Here we investigated the impact of Hurricane Helene on AGI and determined if this impact was different in areas with greater proportions of residents using private wells. We used electronic health records from Truveta to identify inpatient and outpatient visits to hospitals for AGI in NC from 2016-2024 at the zip3-by-week level and classified exposure to flooding using satellite-derived flood depth estimates. We conducted a controlled interrupted time series analysis to estimate the effect of the hurricane on the incidence of AGI among flooded zip3 units. From 2017 to 2024, there were approximately 548k AGI visits in NC across 20 zip3 units. Our findings show that the hurricane was associated with positive, insignificant changes in the incidence of AGI three weeks following the hurricane (incidence rate ratio: 1.11 [0.59, 2.07]), controlled for pre-hurricane trends and post-hurricane changes in lesser flooded regions. Results were consistent across several time windows and analyses examining sensitivity to geographic data masking, model specification, and study design. Our findings warrant re-evaluation at finer spatial and temporal scales and examination of other public health impacts of hurricanes, which are expected to increase in severity and frequency in the eastern United States due to climate change.

after.title: Preprint: Circulating miRNA profiling identifies hsa-miR-23a-3p and a three-miRNA signature associated with serous ovarian cancer
after.authors: Garcia-Llorens, G.; Tierno-Martin, A.; Serra, A.; Gomes-Quiles, L.; Lizano, E.; Sanchez, L.; Llueca, A.; El Ouardi, M.
after.abstract: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC) is the most lethal subtype of epithelial ovarian cancer, highlighting the need for minimally invasive biomarkers that support disease detection and molecular characterization. Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) have emerged as promising candidates, although their clinical applicability remains limited by methodological variability and insufficient validation. Plasma samples from 100 individuals (50 patients with ovarian cancer and 50 cancer-free controls) were initially collected from four biobanks. Following quality control, 94 samples (47 patients and 47 controls) were included in the final analysis. Eight candidate miRNAs were quantified using RT-qPCR, and relative expression was assessed following global mean normalization. Differential expression was evaluated using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, while discriminatory performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Three-miRNA logistic regression models were additionally explored using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation. Among the eight candidates, hsa-miR-23a-3p exhibited significantly lower circulating expression in patients with ovarian cancer than in controls (p = 2.14 x 10^-5), achieving an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.755 (95% CI, 0.657-0.852), with 93.6% sensitivity and 53.2% specificity at the selected threshold. Exploratory analysis across FIGO stages revealed heterogeneous expression patterns, although the limited number of early-stage cases precluded definitive conclusions regarding stage-specific performance. A three-miRNA signature comprising hsa-miR-23a-3p, hsa-miR-21-5p, and hsa-miR-20a-5p achieved an apparent AUC of 0.798. However, repeated cross-validation yielded a mean AUC of 0.716 +/- 0.022, indicating reduced performance after internal validation. Variability in exogenous spike-in Ct values and the marked imbalance in biobank representation between study groups highlighted potential pre-analytical confounding. Circulating hsa-miR-23a-3p showed moderate discriminatory performance between patients with ovarian cancer and cancer-free controls, supporting its further investigation as a candidate liquid biopsy biomarker. Although combining three miRNAs improved apparent classification performance, this advantage was not established through internal validation. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for sample provenance, technical variability, and model overfitting when evaluating circulating miRNA signatures. Independent validation in appropriately balanced cohorts is required before clinical applicability can be established.

after.title: Preprint: LCatlas: A Point-Of-Care Tool for Predicting Immunotherapy Outcomes in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
after.authors: Park, S. Y.; Leyba, A.; Yeung, W.; Hsu, R. C.; Nieva, J.; Lee, H. Y.
after.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality, with a minority of patients experiencing durable responses to first-line immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Currently, there are no easily accessible tools to predict clinical benefit to first-line immunotherapy. To address this gap, we developed LCatlas (https://www.lcatlas.org), a point-of-care web application designed to predict immunotherapy outcomes and inform evidence-based treatment decisions. Using data from 79 NSCLC patients receiving first-line immunotherapy, we extracted demographic, clinical, and molecular features from electronic medical records and compared three independent approaches, statistical model (logistic regression), machine learning (XGboost), and AI model (TabTransformer) to identify the most effective predictor. LCatlas accepts nine variables, gender, smoking history, bone/pleura/liver metastasis, PDL1 tumor staining, albumin level, hemoglobin level, lymphocyte count, neutrophil count, and platelet count, to predict responses to both immunotherapy and immunotherapy plus chemotherapy. LCatlas cross-validation yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 79% [72% - 85%], with sensitivity of 87% [72% - 95%] and specificity of 78% [64% - 89%], outperforming previous studies including high-volume data-driven deep-learning approaches. In a validation cohort consisting of 28 individuals, it demonstrated a prediction accuracy of 82%. LCatlas may serve as a valuable point-of-care tool by identifying patients likely to experience extended immunotherapy or combination therapy using readily available medical data. Its evidence-based approach can optimize personalized treatment planning and thereby promote quality and safety of care.

after.title: Preprint: Development and external validation of a nomogram for predicting re-fracture after percutaneous kyphoplasty: A two-center study
after.authors: Wu, W.; Cui, W.
after.abstract: Background: To identify independent risk factors for subsequent vertebral re-fracture after percutaneous kyphoplasty (PKP) in patients with osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture (OVCF) and to develop and externally validate a predictive nomogram for individualized risk assessment. Methods: This two-center retrospective study enrolled 1,720 OVCF patients who underwent PKP between January 2023 and April 2025. The training cohort (n=963) and internal validation cohort (n=413) were derived from Beijing LUHE Hospital, while the external validation cohort (n=344) was from the other participating center. The primary outcome was postoperative re-fracture confirmed by imaging within a minimum 12-month follow-up. To find independent risk variables in the training cohort, multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed after potential predictors were screened using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Based on these variables, a nomogram was created. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA) were used to evaluate model performance for each of the three cohorts. Results: Five independent factors of re-fracture were found using multivariate logistic regression: advanced age ([≥]65 years) (OR=2.58, 95% CI: 1.81-3.67), body mass index (BMI) [≥]18.5 (protective, OR=0.32, 95% CI: 0.21-0.49), bone mineral density (BMD) (OR=0.13, 95% CI: 0.08-0.20), osteocalcin (BGP) (OR=1.16, 95% CI: 1.09-1.22), and Cobb angle correction (OR=1.36, 95% CI: 1.21-1.53). The nomogram demonstrated good discrimination in the training cohort (AUC=0.810, 95% CI: 0.779-0.841), internal validation cohort (AUC=0.801, 95% CI: 0.732-0.870), and external validation cohort (AUC=0.809, 95% CI: 0.750-0.867). DCA verified net benefit over a threshold probability range of 0-0.6, and calibration curves demonstrated good agreement between projected and observed probabilities. Conclusion: The externally validated nomogram, incorporating age, BMI, BMD, BGP, and Cobb angle correction, provides a robust and practical tool for individualized prediction of re-fracture risk after PKP in OVCF patients, which could facilitate risk-stratified postoperative management and potentially improve patient outcomes. Keywords: Osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture; Percutaneous kyphoplasty; Re-fracture; Risk factors; Nomogram.

The present study investigated whether fibromyalgia (FM) patients have a heightened attention…

after.title: Preprint: Can far become near? The effect of approaching visual stimuli on tactile processing in fibromyalgia patients and controls
after.authors: De Paepe, A. L.; Crombez, G.; Legrain, V.
after.abstract: Within the space closely surrounding us (i.e. the peripersonal space), stimuli on the body surface are integrated with stimuli in the external world. This enables us to interact with the world, and to defend ourselves against potentially threatening objects approaching our body. It has been shown that attention towards stimuli approaching us can differ depending on, for example, the level of anxiety. The present study investigated whether fibromyalgia (FM) patients have a heightened attention to stimuli entering the peripersonal space compared to healthy control participants. This was done by investigating the differential influence of dynamical visual stimuli approaching the body on tactile processing for control participants versus FM patients. For control participants we found, in accordance with previous research, that visual stimuli presented near as opposed to far from the body influenced tactile processing more. For FM patients this difference was less clear, possibly indicating that FM patients have more attention for potentially threatening stimuli at further distance. The curves describing the reaction times along the continuous spatial range (from near to far) indicated that FM patients have a heightened attention for stimuli entering the peripersonal space compared to controls. However, as this difference was only found when curve-fitting the data, we argue that our results should be interpreted with caution and need further corroboration and replication.

after.authors: Zeng, Y.; Cook, N.; Fujita, M.; Johnson, M.; Wingo, A. P.; Wingo, T. S.; DeCasien, A. R.; Pottier, C.; Cruchaga, C.; Menon, V.; Belloy, M. E.
after.abstract: The impact of X-chromosome dosage on gene regulation in specific brain cell-types may importantly shape sex differences in neurodegenerative diseases but remains poorly resolved. We therefore mapped X-chromosome genetic effects on gene expression, i.e. cis-expression quantitative trait loci (cis-eQTL), across seven brain cell-types from 423 old-age individuals. We identified 212 X-linked genes whose expression was genetically regulated, with the majority being cell-type specific. Notably, 10 of these genes (~5%) showed sex-heterogeneous genetic regulation. Through sex-differential expression analyses we further discovered 101 sex-biased genes that were predominantly female-upregulated most strikingly in microglia. Sex-biased gene expression showed both shared and distinct cell-type effects, appearing most divergent in non-neuronal populations. Many female-biased genes overlapped known escape-from-X-inactivation genes and were enriched for links to Alzheimer's disease. Finally, we integrated our resource with X-chromosome-wide association studies of neurodegenerative diseases through causal inference approaches including transcriptome-wide association, mendelian randomization, and colocalization analyses to nominate 11 candidate causal genes, linked to their respective cell-types and sex-informed mechanisms, for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Multiple System Atrophy. Altogether, our findings suggest escape from X chromosome inactivation may contribute to sex differences in neurodegeneration and provide a resource to advance sex-informed insights into disease pathogenesis and therapeutic opportunities.

after.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is common, heritable (h2 ~50%) and polygenic, but the contribution of rare structural variation is largely unexamined. Using short-read whole-genome sequencing (srWGS) data from the All of Us Research Program, we tested the association of rare copy number variants (rCNV; minor allele frequency <1%) with AUD in 56,062 participants (5,410 cases, 50,652 controls) defined from electronic health records. Analyses were conducted within European-like (EUR; N=29,392), African-like (AFR; N=8,269) and Admixed American-like (AMR; N=8,049) samples and combined by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We tested genome-wide rCNV burden, burden within AUD-related, mouse behavioral and neuropsychiatric gene sets, and individual rCNV regions. No genome-wide burden metric or individual rCNV region [≥]10 kb was associated with AUD after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Significant gene-set results were almost exclusively duplications associated with reduced AUD risk across biologically unrelated sets, suggesting a global duplication dosage effect rather than pathway-specific enrichment. In contrast, deletion count within a Neurof_UnionStringent gene set was associated with increased AUD risk (OR=1.04, FDR=0.044), and deletions in xenobiotic-response genes showed nominal associations in multiple ancestry groups. Among rCNV of all sizes, a 58 bp deletion at 16p12.1, a dosage-sensitive neuropsychiatric locus, was significant in the cross-ancestry analysis (OR=2.93, FDR=0.030) without significant heterogeneity. rCNV detectable by srWGS do not appear to contribute substantially to AUD liability at current sample sizes.

after.authors: Khoshnevis, A.; Zayernouri, M.; Malete, L.; Joachim, D.; Ricketts, C.; Ocansey, R.; Muomah, R. C.; Tladi, D.; Ndabi, J. S.; Naghibolhosseini, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Communicative Sciences and Disorders, Michigan State University
after.abstract: This study evaluated machine learning models for screening elevated generalized anxiety symptoms from remotely collected neutral read speech in 1,788 adults from Botswana, Ghana, Nigeria, and Tanzania. Elevated symptoms were defined by Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item (GAD-7) questionnaire scores [≥] 5. Nine classifiers were assessed across nine scenarios defined by speech-task configuration (short sentence, long passage, or both tasks) and sex stratification under participant-separated, repeated nested cross-validation (CV). Acoustic-only models used the extended Geneva Minimalistic Acoustic Parameter Set, and context-augmented models added age, self-reported health, and sex where applicable. With feature selection, the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCROC) was 0.594 for acoustic-only models and 0.699 for context-augmented models, the latter in the female-only combined-task scenario. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) identified fundamental frequency descriptors as prominent acoustic predictors, while health status and age were the leading predictors in context-augmented models. Performance varied across scenarios, and feature selection provided no consistent benefit. Secondary regression poorly estimated continuous symptom severity. These findings indicate limited discrimination from neutral speech acoustics alone and improved performance with participant context, warranting external validation.

after.authors: Reiss, R. N.; Tamara, K. L.; Honnen, W.; Modi, N.; Suarez Caceres, L.; Dendukuri, N.; Schiller, I.; Kaipilyawar, V. S.; Eichberg, C.; Nakiyingi, L.; Centner, C.; Dorman, S.; Ellner, J.; Johnson, W. E.; Salgame, P.; Pinter, A.; Xie, Y. L.
after.abstract: Abstract Background: Culture-negative TB is a major diagnostic challenge, and the lack of a reliable reference standard hinders evaluation of non-sputum diagnostic tests. We compared composite reference criteria and Bayesian latent class analysis to examine how different culture-negative TB definitions affect disease classification and evaluations of two non-sputum biomarkers: urine lipoarabinomannan (uLAM) and host transcriptional response signatures (HRS). Methods: Urine and blood samples from 112 sputum culture-negative and 55 culture-positive symptomatic adults evaluated for tuberculosis from South Africa, Uganda, and Kenya, alongside 17 controls with other respiratory conditions, were analyzed using uLAM and HRS assays. Sensitivity and specificity were estimated for each assay based on three reference criteria: composite microbiological, composite clinical, and a latent class model. Results: Positive classification proportions were 0.29 (32/112) and 0.46 (51/112) for the composite criteria and 0.20 (22/112) for the latent class model, with the Bayesian model estimating a prevalence of 0.31 (95%CrI 0.11-0.64). Sensitivity and specificity for uLAM ranged from 0.06-0.13 and 0.92-0.96, respectively. Sensitivity and specificity for HRS ranged from 0.47-0.78 and 0.56-0.69, respectively. uLAM results were significantly associated with microbiological positivity (OR=5.38, 95%CI=1.63-13.02). Conclusion: Three distinct reference frameworks identified different individuals as having culture-negative TB while producing index assay sensitivity and specificity estimates with overlapping confidence and credible intervals, leading to similar conclusions regarding biomarker utility. This supports the use of complementary reference approaches to assess robustness to disease classification uncertainty in heterogeneous conditions such as culture-negative TB.

after.title: Preprint: Clinician gaze as a supervisory signal for electrocardiogram deep learning: a matched-control proof-of-concept study
after.authors: Mukherjee, A.; Shergill, S.; Ang, C. S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Kent and Medway Medical School, University of Kent, Canterbury, UK
after.abstract: Aims To assess what evidence is required to attribute an apparent effect of clinician-gaze supervision on an electrocardiogram (ECG) deep-learning model to gaze itself, separating target engagement, case specificity, and diagnostic preservation. Methods and results Ten ECG stimuli interpreted by 63 readers yielded 12-lead gaze targets for nine consultants and 20 clinicians. A pretrained 23-output ECG network was fine-tuned with gaze-only loss on eight ECGs per cross-validation fold. Held-out gaze cosine improved modestly (consultants 0.858 to 0.872; all clinicians 0.884 to 0.898), but untrained training-fold mean gaze agreed better (0.929 and 0.951). Lead-occlusion concordance was weak (mean Spearman {rho} 0.236). On 2,198 PTB-XL fold-10 ECGs, macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) fell from 0.922 to 0.893 after gaze-only tuning; uniform and permuted controls also reduced performance. In a post hoc experiment combining PTB-XL diagnostic cross-entropy with gaze loss, macro AUROC was approximately 0.923 in diagnostic-only, real-gaze, uniform and permuted arms, but real-gaze targets were barely fitted even on training ECGs (cosine 0.858 to 0.860). Conclusion In this sparse experiment, gaze-only optimisation engaged its target without demonstrating case-specific learning beyond a population viewing prior, and matched controls showed that the resulting diagnostic deterioration was not attributable to correctly matched gaze. Joint training preserved source-domain discrimination, but because gaze targets were barely fitted, whether gaze adds diagnostic value remains untested. Claims that human viewing has shaped a model require mean-gaze, matched-null and function-preserving controls.

after.authors: Noh, S. A.; Bae, N. Y.; Lim, J.; Kwak, S.; Bak, M.; Park, J.; Choi, H.-M.; Park, J.-B.; Yoon, Y. E.; Lee, S.-P.; Park, J.-H.; Kim, Y.-J.; Cho, G.-Y.; Kim, H.-K.; Hwang, I.-C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Cardiology, Cardiovascular Center, Seoul National University Bundang  Hospital, Republic of Korea
after.abstract: Background: The cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) framework emphasizes risk assessment and prevention of heart failure (HF). However, the prognostic implications and optimal assessment of CKM burden in established HF remain uncertain. Objectives: To evaluate the prognostic value of binary and HF-adapted graded CKM burden scores across HF phenotypes. Methods: We evaluated 2 independent HF cohorts comprising patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) initiating angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor therapy (HFrEF-ARNI; n=1,450) and patients hospitalized for acute HF (AHF; n = 2,985). AHF patients were stratified by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) into <50% and [≥]50% (HFrEF and HF with preserved ejection fraction [HFpEF] groups, respectively). The binary score counted 6 CKM components; the graded score incorporated chronic kidney disease severity and reverse-scored body mass index categories. Associations with the composite outcome of all-cause death or HF hospitalization were assessed using Cox regression. Prognostic discrimination and interactions with HF phenotype were also evaluated. Results: Median follow-up was 31.5 months in HFrEF-ARNI and 51.1 months in AHF. Both scores were independently associated with the composite outcome in both cohorts. In HFrEF-ARNI cohort, adjusted HRs per 1-point increase were 1.10 (95% CI 1.02-1.18) for the binary score and 1.11 (95% CI 1.04-1.19) for the graded score. In AHF, both scores were associated with outcomes in HFrEF, whereas only the graded score was significantly associated with the outcome in HFpEF (binary: HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.90-1.02; graded: HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.04-1.15). Significant interactions with HF phenotype were observed for both scores. The graded score showed better discrimination than the binary score in both cohorts (C-index 0.632 vs 0.583 in HFrEF-ARNI; 0.609 vs 0.541 in AHF), particularly in HFpEF (C-index 0.576 vs 0.491). In HFpEF, only the graded score provided significant incremental prognostic information beyond clinical and echocardiographic variables ({chi}2 = 11.3; P <0.001). Conclusions: The HF-adapted graded CKM burden score demonstrated more consistent prognostic associations and better risk discrimination than the binary score, particularly in HFpEF. Incorporating disease severity and HF-relevant prognostic characteristics may refine CKM burden assessment and risk stratification in established HF.

after.authors: Kloetzsch, A.-T.; Kuehl, T.; Christ, M.; Hailer, B.; Frank, B.; Koehrmann, M.; Kleinschnitz, C.; Bruder, O.; Stang, A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Institute for Biometrics and Epidemiology, German Diabetes Center, Leibniz Center for Diabetes Research at Heinrich Heine University, Duesseldorf, Germany
after.abstract: Studies of myocardial infarction and stroke showed a diurnal variation with peaks in the morning and afternoon. So far, night sleep or napping have not been investigated as triggers for cardiovascular events via a case-crossover study. Therefore, the main question of the ACROSSS (Acute CoROnary Syndrome, Stroke and Sleep) study is how much the occurrence of a myocardial infarction/stroke/transient ischemic attack is associated with taking a nap shortly before (topic 1, case-crossover study, 656 patients needed). Moreover, the study aims at assessing the incidence of sleep disturbances three and twelve months after a myocardial infarction/stroke/transient ischemic attack (topic 2, follow-up study, 400 patients needed). Recruitment of patients is carried out in four German hospitals in Essen and Bottrop, North Rhine-Westphalia. The examination program includes the case-crossover questionnaire on potential acute triggers of cardiovascular events, a sleep questionnaire with validated instruments (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, etc.) and a questionnaire on health status and lifestyle habits. Moreover, eligible patients are screened for sleep apnea and during the follow-up sleep is measured by actigraphy. The combination of sleep-related and clinical data offers a deeper understanding of how sleep affects the acute onset of a cardiovascular event and recovery afterwards.

after.authors: Mak, H. W.; Li, K.; Makridis, C. A.; Chen, Y.; Weziak-Bialowolska, D.; Kim, E. S.; Fancourt, D.
after.abstract: Arts and cultural engagement is increasingly recognised as a potential resource for health and wellbeing, yet evidence remains dominated by Western, high-income countries. Using data from the Global Flourishing Study across 22 countries (N=118,045), we examined associations between arts engagement and 19 health and wellbeing outcomes across five domains, applying an outcome-wide analytical framework and random-effects meta-analysis. Arts engagement was consistently associated with greater positive wellbeing and character strengths, higher evaluative wellbeing, and better social and general health, including lower loneliness. By contrast, associations with future-oriented wellbeing and perceived capability were less robust, and no pooled associations emerged for psychological distress. Country-level characteristics explained little cross-national variation. These findings suggest that arts engagement may promote flourishing across diverse cultural contexts, with benefits extending beyond the prevention of psychological distress, highlighting its potential role as a global population health resource.

after.authors: Tzoref, A.; Dichter, A.; Meiri, G.; Menashe, I.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Epidemiology, Biostatistics and Community Health Sciences, Faculty of Health Sciences, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Beer-Sheva, Israel
after.abstract: Background: Maternal immune activation is a robust risk factor for autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Current evidence relies on specialized immunological markers not routinely measured, limiting population-level risk identification. We investigated the association between maternal white blood cell (WBC) counts, a ubiquitous component of routine prenatal care during pregnancy, and offspring ASD risk. Methods: We conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study of 303,234 singleton live births (51% male) between 2011 and 2021 from Clalit Health Services in Israel. Exposures were maternal total and differential WBC counts from routine testing during the 1st and 2nd trimesters. High and low exposures were defined as >97.5th and <2.5th percentiles, respectively. The primary outcome was clinical ASD diagnosis. Analyses included multivariable logistic regressions, matched-sibling analyses (n=2,894 discordant pairs), and chronicity analyses in multiparous mothers (n=72,102). Results: Among 303,234 children, 8,106 (2.7%) were diagnosed with ASD. Elevated maternal total WBC counts were associated with increased odds of ASD (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]=1.59; 95% CI, 1.43-1.75), with the strongest association in the 1st trimester (aOR=1.64; 95% CI, 1.45-1.85). Similar associations were seen with elevated neutrophils, lymphocytes, and monocytes. While most associations were attenuated in matched-sibling analyses, chronicity analysis revealed increased ASD odds in offspring of mothers with persistently elevated WBC counts across multiple pregnancies (aOR=1.49; 95% CI, 1.08-2.01). Conclusions: Persistently elevated maternal WBC counts across pregnancies are associated with increased offspring ASD risk. These routinely collected hematologic markers support the maternal immune activation hypothesis and may contribute to future prenatal risk assessment models.

after.abstract: Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is an increasingly prevalent neurodevelopmental condition with multifactorial origins, including potential prenatal environmental contributions. Maternal anemia (decreased hemoglobin [Hb] levels) has long been associated with adverse offspring neurodevelopmental outcomes. Yet, evidence regarding elevated levels of antenatal hemoglobin levels, in relation to ASD risk remains limited. This study evaluated the association between maternal Hb levels during pregnancy and the risk of ASD diagnosis in offspring. Methods This large-scale, population-based retrospective cohort study used electronic health records from births of members of Clalit Health Services (CHS), the largest health maintenance organization in Israel, between 2011 and 2021. The study included 303,234 singleton live births to Jewish mothers who had at least one measured prenatal Hb value and were CHS members. Exclusion criteria were children with known genetic disorders and births <25 weeks of gestation. Maternal Hb, and red blood cells (RBC) levels during the first and second trimesters were categorized as low (<2.5th percentile), normal (reference), or high (>97.5th percentile). The main outcome was a diagnosis of ASD in the offspring, as recorded in medical files. Statistical analyses adjusted for maternal age, socioeconomic status, gestational diabetes, BMI, and other clinical and demographic factors. Results Among the 303,234 births, 8,106 (2.7%) children were diagnosed with ASD. High maternal Hb levels were associated with elevated odds of ASD diagnosis (aOR=1.22; 95% CI=1.08:1.37), with the strongest association observed for first-trimester measurements (aOR=1.31; 95% CI=1.14-1.49). This association persisted in the sibling-matched analysis (aOR=1.64; 95% CI=1.08-2.47) and was not modified by maternal RBC levels, suggesting that it was not explained by familial factors or RBC counts. The main limitations of this study include the lack of available data on maternal smoking, and the absence of detailed information on maternal nutritional status. Conclusions These findings suggest that elevated antenatal Hb levels may be relevant to offspring neurodevelopment. Further studies are needed to replicate these findings and clarify the biological mechanisms underlying this association.

after.abstract: Introduction: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is a clinical condition influenced by several socioeconomic, demographic and anthropometric factors, especially if patients are on hemodialysis (HD). Objective: Analyze the QoL in patients with chronic kidney disease on hemodialysis. Methodology: The study was developed with 52 patients with chronic kidney disease undergoing hemodialysis at the SC LTDA Nephrology Clinic, at the Hospital Regional of Ararangua, Santa Catarina. The patients' quality of life was quantified in domains obtained through the KDQOL-SF 1.3 questionnaire, which analyzes several aspects, including: impacts of the disease on physical and mental health, impact of the disease on daily activities and satisfaction with treatment. Another questionnaire, authored by the researchers, containing socioeconomic, demographic and anthropometric data was also applied. Finally, the results of the two questionnaires were related to see which factors influence QoL and how.

after.title: Preprint: Distinct Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging-Derived White Matter Microstructural Phenotypes Tracking Alzheimer's Disease Pathology and Cognitive Decline
after.authors: Yablonskiy, D.; Kothapalli, S. V.; Eldeniz, C.; Morris, J. C.; Benzinger, T. L. S.
after.abstract: White matter (WM) pathology is increasingly recognized as an early, mechanistically relevant feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet sensitive in-vivo biomarkers remain limited. Here, we introduce an MRI-based Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) technique sensitive to WM microstructure. RKI metrics differentiate two distinct phenotypes of white matter that follow divergent microstructural trajectories in preclinical and early symptomatic AD. We examined their relationships to AD progression, gray matter (GM) pathology, and clinical impairment in 305 adults spanning amyloid-negative to amyloid-positive stages with normal cognition, preclinical AD, and early symptomatic AD. Pathological changes in one phenotype reflected axonal alterations without myelin loss and were anatomically coupled to GM cortical pathology, strengthening with disease stage - a signature of Wallerian degeneration. Alterations in the other phenotype represented WM demyelination. A model incorporating RKI-metrics, age, sex, amyloid status, APOE genotype, and brain volume classified Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-based impairment with an area under the receiver operating curve (AUC) = 0.933, with the RKI-metrics contributing 27% (second only to amyloid at 40%). While both phenotypes related comparably to concurrent cognition (each ~27%), the "axonal" phenotype showed the strongest relationship to subsequent cognitive decline (41% of explained variance), with the "myelin" phenotype contributing 31%. These RKI-defined dual white matter phenotypes provide new insight into AD pathology, adding diagnostic and prognostic value for tracking both current cognitive status and future cognitive decline.

after.authors: Jaraj, D.; Eliasdottir, O.; Winblad, S.; Lindberg, C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Sahlgrenska Academy, University of Gothenburg, Sahlgrenska University Hopsital
after.abstract: Introduction: Respiratory complications are a leading cause mortality in myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), making it essential to identify modifiable factors that influence long-term pulmonary function. Vitamin D is known to have an important role in muscle physiology, but its potential relevance for respiratory muscle function has previously not been examined in this patient population. Methods: This was a prospective cohort study including patients with genetically verified DM1 (n = 127) aged 18 years or more. Mean follow-up was 4.3 years. All patients underwent a series of examinations including blood tests and measurement of Vitamin D levels and Forced vital capacity % of predicted (FVC%). Results: Vitamin D insufficiency (<50 nmol/L) was present in 43% of participants. Mean FVC% decreased modestly from 65.7% to 63.6% during follow-up (p=0.004). Patients with vitamin D insufficiency had significantly lower FVC% at follow-up compared to those with sufficient levels (54.7% vs 71.2%, p<0.001), and a higher proportion had worsened FVC% (72% vs 50%, p=0.04). In multivariable regression analyses adjusted for disease severity, lower vitamin D levels were independently associated with worse FVC% at follow-up ({beta}=0.12, p=0.04). When vitamin D was examined as a categorical variable in an adjusted model, patients with insufficiency had on average 4.2 percentage points lower FVC% at follow-up compared to those with sufficient levels ({beta}=-4.17, p=0.018), independent of baseline lung function and disease severity. Discussion: Lower baseline Vitamin D levels were strongly related to lung function at follow-up in patients with DM1. These findings remained significant after adjusting for potential confounders. However, because FVC% remained largely stable during follow-up, the possibility to assess the long-term effects of vitamin D on change in respiratory function was limited.

after.title: Preprint: ProbeFit: one-seizure qualification and personalisation of multimodal wearable seizure detectors
after.authors: Cui, H.; Zhu, Y.; Huang, S.; Xu, T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Biomedical Engineering, College of Engineering, Shantou University, Shantou, Guangdong, China
after.abstract: Background and Objective: Missed seizures hinder assessment of seizure frequency and treatment. Although wearables can detect seizures automatically, performance varies between patients. Before deployment, it remains difficult to identify suitable patients, and personalisation usually requires several recorded seizures. We propose ProbeFit to predict later seizure sensitivity and personalise a wearable detector from the first recorded seizure. Methods: We used multicentre SeizeIT2 recordings of behind-the-ear EEG, ECG, EMG and movement from 125 patients. Two generic detectors' peak responses to the first seizure generated a qualification probability. The same seizure and preceding background personalised the detector. ProbeFit was developed on 96 patients and applied unchanged to 29 held-out patients. Expert-labelled video-EEG seizures provided the reference. Evaluation compared qualification with the first-seizure heart-rate rule and measured discrimination, calibration and net benefit, and it compared later sensitivity of the generic and personalised detectors at equal false-alarm rates. Results: Among 27 held-out patients with 152 later seizures, qualification correlated with later sensitivity at Spearman {rho} = 0.38, with one-sided p = 0.033. It identified patients with later sensitivity [≥] 0.5 with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.74. Across all 97 evaluable patients, AUC was 0.76 against 0.59 for the heart-rate rule, a difference of 0.17 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.05 to 0.29. At the qualification threshold of 0.5, ProbeFit withheld deployment from 9 of 15 held-out patients below the sensitivity criterion, and its net benefit was 0.074 against -0.111 for selecting everyone. At equal false-alarm rates between 0.25 and 2 per day, personalisation raised later sensitivity by 2.2 percentage points in held-out patients and by 6.3 points in development patients. Both confidence intervals excluded zero, and no held-out patient lost sensitivity. Conclusions: ProbeFit uses the first recorded seizure to predict whether a wearable detector will detect at least half of a patient's later seizures, and it personalises that detector without waiting for further seizures. It supports patient selection and adaptation during the first monitoring admission.

after.title: Preprint: Stakeholder perspectives on community-based nutrition interventions for child stunting in Rwanda: A qualitative comparative study of caregivers, health workers and health service managers
after.authors: Ntawuyirushintege, S.; Mohamed, N. S.; Ahmed, A.; Rulisa, S.; Remera, E.; Wyss, K.
after.abstract: Stunting among children under 2 years old remains a major public health concern in Rwanda despite the efforts to reduce its prevalence. Community-based nutrition interventions, including food supplementation, growth monitoring, screening and referral, are widely delivered, yet high coverage has not consistently translated into lower stunting prevalence. This study explores caregivers, community health workers (CHWs), and health service managers experiences and understanding of these interventions. A qualitative descriptive study was conducted in the areas of Bugeshi (Rubavu district) and Rugarama (Nyarugenge district) health centres, purposively selected for their contrasting district stunting trajectories. We conducted six focus group discussions with caregivers and CHWs (48 participants) and 21 in-depth interviews with facility-based nutritionists and environmental health officers, local health service managers, and national, international and private-sector programme managers and experts. Data analysis using reflexive thematic analysis showed seven emerging themes, including competing explanations for persistent stunting; experiences of receiving and using food supplements; the emotional and social dimensions of malnutrition; the central but under-resourced, and at times unsafe, role of CHWs; difficulties in reaching eligible children; governance and financial sustainability; and supply chain constraints. All groups valued food supplementation and shared an understanding of stunting. Caregivers and frontline CHWs more often described problems at the point of delivery such as eligible children being missed, supplements being shared with siblings and other household members or being unavailable, and CHWs facing hostility during periods of stock-outs. Managers and programme experts emphasised financing, procurement and distribution as essential pillar for intervention success. Community-based nutrition interventions were widely valued, but participants described a substantial gap between programme design and day-to-day implementation. Strengthening implementation will require attention to the working conditions of CHWs, household economic realities, programme eligibility criteria, supply and financing systems, and routine use of caregiver and CHWs feedback in programme monitoring.

after.title: Preprint: A pilot study of the mutational landscape of colorectal cancer in Black South Africans
after.authors: Brandenburg, J.-T.; Campbell, L.; Engelbrecht, D.; Mathew, C. G.; Thompson, G.; Moonsamy, D.; Harran, N.; Martin, R.; Bebington, B.; Soldati, V.; Perdomo, S.; Stevens, W.; Fabian, J.; Haycock, P.; MOSAIC,
after.abstract: **Background:** Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa, where the molecular landscape of the disease remains poorly characterised. In particular, genomic studies of resident Black African populations are limited, and the contribution of population-specific mutational processes and potential infectious exposures remains insufficiently understood. The Molecular, Somatic and Infectious Drivers of Colorectal Cancer in Africa (MOSAIC) collaboration aims to address these gaps by generating population-specific genomic data. This pilot study aimed to assess the feasibility of paired tumour-normal whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and to provide an initial characterisation of somatic mutations and mutational signatures in South African patients with CRC. **Methods:** We recruited five Black South African patients with newly diagnosed, treatment-naive CRC through the CoRecT Cancer study at Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital and Wits University Donald Gordon Medical Centre, Johannesburg. Fresh-frozen colorectal tumour tissue and matched peripheral blood samples were subjected to paired-end WGS (2 x 151 bp) using the Illumina NovaSeq X Plus platform. Somatic variants were identified using CaVEMan and Strelka2, followed by functional annotation using the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP). Protein-altering variants were characterised using the R package maftools. Mutational signature contributions were estimated using SigProfilerAssignment and the COSMIC v3 reference catalogue. **Results:** All ten sequencing samples, comprising five tumour-blood pairs, passed quality control. Estimated sequencing depth ranged from 49.2X to 82.4X for tumour samples and from 22.7X to 40.7X for matched blood samples, with a median of 96.3% well-aligned reads. Following somatic variant calling and filtering, the number of retained mutations ranged from 1,106 to 65,379 per tumour. Three of the five tumours harboured at least one predicted protein-altering variant, comprising seven missense and four splice-site variants across eleven genes. Mutational signature analysis of single base substitutions (SBS) revealed inter-individual heterogeneity. SBS1 and SBS5 were detected across all five tumours, while additional signatures included SBS18, SBS20, SBS26 and SBS44, among others. Several tumours exhibited signatures associated with mismatch repair-related mutational processes. **Conclusions:** This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of paired tumour-normal WGS and preliminary somatic mutation profiling in Black South African patients with CRC. The findings provide initial insights into the heterogeneous mutational landscape of CRC in this underrepresented population. However, the small sample size and incomplete clinical and molecular characterisation necessitate cautious interpretation. Larger studies incorporating comprehensive mismatch repair assessment, copy-number and structural variant analysis, germline susceptibility profiling and investigation of infectious exposures will be essential to validate these preliminary observations and better understand the molecular and environmental drivers of CRC in African populations.

Three of the five tumours harboured at least one predicted protein-altering variant, comprising seven missense and four splice-site variants across eleven genes. Mutational signature analysis of single base substitutions (SBS) revealed inter-individual heterogeneity. SBS1 and SBS5 were detected across all five tumours, while additional signatures included SBS18, SBS20, SBS26 and SBS44, among others. Several tumours exhibited signatures associated with mismatch repair-related mutational processes. **Conclusions:** This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of paired tumour-normal WGS and preliminary somatic mutation profiling in Black South African patients with CRC. The findings provide initial insights into the heterogeneous mutational landscape of CRC in this underrepresented population. However, the small sample size and incomplete clinical and molecular characterisation necessitate cautious interpretation. Larger studies incorporating comprehensive mismatch repair assessment, copy-number and structural variant analysis, germline susceptibility profiling and investigation of infectious exposures will be essential to validate these preliminary observations and better understand the molecular and environmental drivers of CRC in African populations.

after.abstract: We evaluated whether germline genomic risk complements prostate-specific antigen (PSA) for prostate cancer early detection. P-CARE integrates a 601-variant polygenic hazard score, family history, and genetic ancestry. Long-term outcomes and clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection on biopsy were assessed in the Million Veteran Program (MVP), with external validation in the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial (PCPT). Among 428,512 MVP participants, high versus low P-CARE risk was associated with increased hazards of treatment (HR 3.32) and metastasis (HR 3.32). Among men whose baseline PSA was measured at ages 40-49 with PSA 1-3 ng/mL, 15-year treatment/metastasis probabilities were 2.6%, 4.5%, and 10.2% across increasing P-CARE risk groups. High P-CARE risk also predicted csPCa on biopsy (OR 2.96), while PRSPSA was inversely associated with outcomes. Findings were consistent in PCPT. Germline genomic risk complements measured PSA, supporting prospective evaluation of genetically informed screening strategies.

after.abstract: How inherited genetic variation propagates through multicellular regulatory systems to influence human disease remains poorly understood. To reconstruct the regulatory architecture of genetic variation on circulating immune cells, we analysed single-cell transcriptomes from 6.7 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 4,452 European-ancestry UK Biobank participants, identifying 114,063 independent cis-regulatory effects affecting 15,419 genes. Using a new statistical workflow (FLANDERS), we map the hierarchical organisation of these effects and the underlying regulatory architecture across tissues, immune lineages, cell types and cell states. We find that disease-associated variants predominantly act through regulatory programmes shared within immune lineages and broad cellular compartments, rather than through highly specific cellular states. We show that local cis -regulatory effects commonly act through coherent regulatory pathways implicating transcription factor cascades and intercellular signalling, which allows linking together multiple disease genes. We demonstrate independent support for these genes and mechanisms through rare variant associations. Our findings reveal a highly organised structure of immune regulatory variation shaping human disease, and provide a highly effective framework for interpreting disease associations and prioritising therapeutic targets.

after.abstract: Human immune composition reflects genetic background and cumulative life-course exposures, yet how these influences shape immune architecture across populations and disease remains poorly understood. Here we integrate single-cell transcriptomics, matched clinical haematology and electronic health records from 5,079 individuals of European, British-Pakistani and British-Bangladeshi ancestries to quantify 26 circulating immune cell types and 62 transcriptional states. We map immune compositional variation associated with age, sex, adiposity and smoking, revealing distinct patterns across adulthood and associations between modifiable exposures and advanced immune age. Across common diseases, immune compositional signatures converge on recurrent inflammatory myeloid, adaptive-memory and interferon programmes, whose expression varies with age and population context. Cardiovascular therapies are associated with selective shifts in disease-associated immune states. Immune composition further discriminates common cardiometabolic diseases and resolves patients into endotypes with distinct metabolic and clinical profiles. These findings establish circulating immune architecture as an integrative phenotype linking life-course exposures, population context and disease, providing a framework for precision population immunology.

after.title: Preprint: Virtual spatial transcriptomics links kidney histopathology to disease-associated molecular programs
after.authors: Nonchev, K.; Jang, Y.; Nlandu Khodo, S.; Koelzer, V. H.; Raetsch, G.; Moor, M. B.
after.abstract: Introduction: Spatial transcriptomics can resolve compartment-specific molecular programs in kidney disease, but its cost and technical requirements limit its use in clinical diagnostics and in large biopsy archives. Predicting spatial gene expression from routine histology with artificial intelligence could extend molecular characterization to existing clinically annotated kidney tissue collections. Methods: We adapted DeepSpot-M, a pretrained multimodal foundation model that predicts spatial gene expression from histology, using paired hematoxylin and eosin images and Visium spatial transcriptomics from 209 Kidney Precision Medicine Project (KPMP) participants. We evaluated virtual profiles in held-out human biopsies, associated them with histopathologic and biochemical injury markers in 567 rats with defined nephrotoxin exposures from a public toxicogenomics database, and generated a virtual atlas from 1,534 histology slides of 476 additional KPMP participants. Results: Kidney-specific adaptation of DeepSpot-M doubled the mean Pearson correlation of each model's 1,000 best-predicted genes (0.43 versus 0.22) and exceeded recent foundation models. Virtual profiles preserved the direction of all 13 disease-marker differences in measured expression, including tubular injury, maladaptive repair, gluconeogenesis, and fibrosis-associated programs. All 11 measured associations between molecular programs and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) were also preserved. Without rat-specific training, a virtual injury score distinguished moderate or severe histopathologic lesions (area under the curve, 0.85) and at least twofold blood urea nitrogen elevation (0.82). In our atlas of 5.46 million virtual spots, higher proximal tubule program scores were associated with higher eGFR (partial r, 0.32) and less interstitial fibrosis (-0.57), and program-pathology associations agreed with those of measured Visium profiles in independent participants (Spearman rho, 0.64). Conclusions: Kidney-adapted virtual spatial transcriptomics links histology-derived molecular programs to experimental renal injury and human clinical and histologic phenotypes. Our approach enables spatial molecular analyses in routine biopsy histology, which could help decipher disease-associated pathways in existing biopsy archives.

after.abstract: Background: According to the -Synuclein Origin site and Connectome (SOC) model, idiopathic Parkinson's Disease (iPD) is classified into two distinct subtypes: symmetric body-first, with diffuse spread and early non-motor clinical manifestations, and asymmetric brain-first, with initially circumscribed motor manifestations. Evidence regarding the application of this model to genetic PD remains limited. Objective: To investigate imaging and motor asymmetry in genetic vs iPD and idiopathic REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (iRBD), addressing thus indirectly the SOC model in genetic PD. Methods: We analyzed demographic, imaging and clinical data from 85 GBA PD, 166 LRRK2 PD, and 912 iPD patients, as well as 30 iRBD participants with abnormal DATSCAN from the PPMI database. Imaging asymmetry was assessed both by Asymmetry Index and absolute Asymmetry difference. Motor asymmetry was calculated as the absolute difference between the MDS-UPDRS III scores of the right and left sides. Results: GBA- and LRRK2-PD patients exhibit more symmetric putaminal radioligand uptake than iPD patients, but greater imaging asymmetry than iRBD subjects in the caudate. iRBD is more symmetric than iPD in both caudate and putamen. Consistent with the imaging data, GBA- and LRRK2-PD exhibit greater clinical motor symmetry than iPD. Conclusion: GBA- and LRRK2-PD are more symmetric than iPD on imaging and clinical grounds. GBA-PD appears to be a predominantly symmetric diffuse synucleinopathy, as predicted by the SOC model. The SOC model may not be applicable to LRRK2-PD, with its predominantly circumscribed motor phenotype, possibly because in this case -Synuclein pathology does not determine lateralization of motor manifestations.

after.abstract: Cervical cancer remains a major public health problem in Nigeria, yet data on high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) across the cervical disease spectrum are limited in Abuja. We conducted a hospital-based comparative cross-sectional study of 101 women aged [≥]25 years at Federal Medical Centre, Abuja: 59 with negative cytology (NILM) and 42 with cervical lesions, comprising 23 low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL), 8 high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL), and 11 invasive cervical cancers. Cervical specimens were tested using the Atila ScreenFire assay, which reports four pooled hrHPV target groups. hrHPV DNA was detected in 37/101 women (36.6%): 30.5% (18/59) with NILM, 26.1% (6/23) with LSIL, 50.0% (4/8) with HSIL, and 81.8% (9/11) with invasive cervical cancer (Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact p=0.005). Compared with NILM, invasive cervical cancer was associated with approximately tenfold higher odds of hrHPV detection (unadjusted odds ratio [OR] 10.25, 95% CI 2.01-52.28; age-adjusted OR 9.90, 95% CI 1.87-52.38). The HPV31/33/35/52/58 target group was detected most frequently overall (12.9%), followed by HPV16 and HPV18/45 (10.9% each), and HPV39/51/56/59/68 (5.9%). HPV16 was the most frequent target group in invasive cervical cancer (5/11). No individual target group was independently associated with lesion status. The NILM and lesion groups differed substantially in ethnicity, religion, and previous cervical screening, indicating different referral and screening pathways; therefore, the NILM group should not be considered population-based. These findings demonstrate marked enrichment of hrHPV in invasive cervical cancer and substantial detection of non-16/18 target groups. They support HPV-based screening, continued genotype surveillance, and larger multicentre studies using population-based comparison groups.

after.authors: Song, J.; Kudrimoti, S.; Jiang, C.; Zhao, J.; Kamgarhaghighi, Y.; Liang, H.; Achacoso, N. S.; Solorzano, A. V.; Tse, P.; Chung, E.; Thomas, S.; Itakura, H.; Ghezelayagh, T.; Habel, L.; Pan, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Internal Medicine Residency Program, Kaiser Permanente, Santa Clara, CA 94051, USA
after.abstract: Objective. To determine whether TP53 and other pathogenic variants (PVs) carry shared or organ-specific prognostic associations in advanced ovarian and endometrial carcinoma. Methods. We analyzed 1060 patients with stage III-IV ovarian carcinoma (924 high-grade serous [HGSOC], 66 clear cell [CCOC], 42 endometrioid, 28 mucinous) and 543 with endometrial carcinoma (EC) profiled by next-generation sequencing. Associations with overall survival (OS) were estimated by multivariable Cox regression and combined across organs by fixed-effect pooling. Key findings were tested in 8881 tumors from public cBioPortal cohorts, including The Cancer Genome Atlas. Results. TP53 PV was associated with worse OS in EC (HR 1.61, 95% CI 1.23-2.10) and CCOC (HR 3.23, 1.05-9.89) but not in HGSOC overall (HR 0.95, 0.72-1.25); in HGSOC, it was associated with worse OS only in KRAS-mutant tumors (HR 3.42, 1.13-10.33). KRAS PV was associated with better OS in CCOC (HR 0.29, 0.09-0.89) and HGSOC (HR 0.72, 0.50-1.02) but not in EC. In HGSOC, BRCA1/2 PV was associated with better OS and MYC amplification with worse OS. In EC, CTNNB1 and ARID1A PVs were associated with better OS. RB1 PV was associated with worse OS in both organs (pooled HR 1.47, 1.05-2.06). In public cohorts stratified by histology, TP53 alteration was associated with worse OS in EC (HR 1.69, 1.36-2.10) and ovarian carcinoma (HR 1.28, 1.00-1.62). Conclusions. The prognostic association of TP53 PV depends on organ, histotype and co-occurring KRAS PV, and RB1 PV is a shared adverse marker. These findings may inform prognostic stratification of Mullerian carcinomas.

items.title: Preprint: Multimodal population-scale cell atlases define archetypes and extremes of human blood

after.abstract: The cellular composition of blood is fundamental to human physiology and is routinely measured to assess health and disease. Circulating immune cells show extensive heterogeneity, but the organising principles and extremes of variation across individuals remain undefined. Here, using single-cell transcriptomics across two biobank cohorts encompassing ~6,000 individuals, we show that human blood occupies recurrent archetypal states defined by coordinated cell composition patterns. We delineate three major archetypes spanning naive lymphoid, myeloid and cytotoxic composition, and two minor archetypes characterised by type I interferon-driven inflammation and expanded premalignant CD5+ B cells. We develop cell2clone to infer lymphocyte clonal expansions, revealing how reactive clonal processes drive the cytotoxic archetype and premalignant clonal expansion establishes the CD5+ B cell archetype, creating outlier states that uncover context-specific effects of germline variants. Clonal haematopoiesis and mosaic chromosomal alterations influence blood states in an archetype-dependent manner. The archetype framework links blood states to common disease risk and clinical blood counts and, through a machine-learning model ArcheTypist, classifies infection and cancer immunotherapy outcomes. This population-scale framework has implications for diagnostics, early disease detection, immunotherapy stratification and mechanistic insights into disease susceptibility and therapy response, providing an organising model for identifying compositional subtypes across human tissues.

after.title: Preprint: MRCAT: A multi-agent framework for reliable Mendelian randomization analysis and causal interpretation
after.authors: JIANG, Y.; Zhang, F.; Huang, X.; Wang, Z.; Hu, X.; Yang, C.
after.abstract: Mendelian randomization (MR) uses genetic variants to estimate causal effects of exposures on health outcomes, but rigorous MR analyses require coordinated procedures and interpretation under explicit methodological assumptions. Although artificial intelligence (AI) agents can automate analyses, computational completion does not guarantee scientific reliability. Here, we present MRCAT, a multi-agent framework that translates MR-specific knowledge into an AI-assisted workflow that is plannable, executable, verifiable, recoverable and traceable. MRCAT combines dependency-aware planning, Skill-guided execution and expert-informed review with traceable reporting guided by STROBE-MR, a guideline for clear and transparent reporting of MR studies, and iterative Writer-Judge checking. We evaluated MRCAT on 30 natural-language queries spanning diverse data sources, analytical requirements and boundary conditions. MRCAT achieved scientific completion, defined as meeting all nine prespecified MR-specific procedural requirements, for all 26 executable queries and appropriately handled all four boundary cases, compared with 17, 11 and 4 scientifically completed queries for Claude Code, Biomni and BioMedAgent, respectively. Across six independently curated tasks for which the expert-curated analyses did not support causal effects, MRCAT showed closer numerical concordance with the expert-curated analyses and produced interpretations consistent with expert-curated conclusions in all six cases, compared with two for Claude Code and four for Biomni. Additional case studies demonstrated evidence-grounded reporting and selective reuse of analytical outputs in multi-exposure and bidirectional MR investigations. MRCAT provides a framework for reducing the operational burden of MR research while supporting reproducible analysis, assumption-consistent interpretation and traceable scientific reporting.
